extracted.intended_audience: teachers, educators, and students of educational theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical criteria for motivating pupils and organising instruction, emphasising the roles of emotions (power, pride, praise), the contrast of individual vs general knowledge, and methods to make abstractions intelligible and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the emotion of power as an educational motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling or emotion of power expresses a first-class motive of the human mind and can be a source of gratification in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'power' often refers to bodily/mental superiority, wealth, or office, may include malevolent elements (love of domineering), but can be expanded ideally (e.g., appreciation of sublime natural forces). Treat the gratification of a pupil's sense of self-activity as an educational motive that requires careful examination before deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harness self-esteem, pride, vanity, and love of applause carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-complacency, pride, vanity, and love of applause are intense feelings especially invoked in education and can promote attainment of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use praise as an instrument: it should be 'carefully apportioned' and 'take place apart from ulterior considerations.' Avoid thoughtless profusion of compliment (which defeats itself) and prefer warm kindly expression when appropriate. Praise establishes future claims and must be measured so it 'approves itself to all concerned.' A pleased smile or simple warm expression can have moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dispraise and loss of esteem as disciplinary tools with delicacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispraise, depreciation, and the loss of estimation can produce powerful self-reproach and are effective disciplinary instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that inducing self-reproach is difficult directly; disciplinary effects often operate through others' estimation. The handling of dispraise must be very delicate as its remission or abatement has immediate and severe effects. High refinements of moral control depend on subtle use of this instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to intellectual emotions but recognize their relative magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasurable emotions from intellectual exercise exist but are typically less intense than social/self feelings; their appeal depends on the kind of knowledge and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discriminate kinds of knowledge (individual/concrete vs general/abstract). Cultivate intrinsic charms of knowledge by connecting intellectual tasks to stronger feelings or by showing practical utility and explanatory power to generate interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach general/abstract knowledge through concrete particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulars are generally interesting and easy; generals are often uninteresting and hard. To teach generalities effectively, use concrete examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide plenty of particulars to illustrate abstract concepts; make generalities bear fruit by applying them in solving problems and shortening intellectual labour. Introduce abstract symbols (formulas, diagrams) only alongside concretes and when pupils have some familiarity with the field where they apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awaken the pleasure of discovering identity among diverse particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'flash of identity in diversity'—seeing likeness among seemingly unlike things—is an exhilarating emotional reward that motivates pursuit of general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure instruction to create opportunities for pupils to detect similarities across different cases (e.g., showing how disparate phenomena share a common cause). Use such discoveries to provide emotional reinforcement and to show explanatory value (e.g., unifying phenomena under a law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical need and application to motivate abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical necessity and the easing of intellectual labour are powerful motives for forming general notions and abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present abstract ideas by reference to practical problems where only certain properties matter (e.g., considering an iron bar as weight or lever). Emphasize how abstraction allows economy of thought and action and how general notions serve practical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit movement/change to engage attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement or change excites interest more than stillness; moving things attract and hold attention more readily than objects at rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, present dynamic examples or emphasize processes and change to arouse curiosity and ease acquisition. Use still-life only when tied to movement or as illustrating underlying change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage analytical separation (abstraction) by isolating relevant properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When using objects as agents in practical operations, we attend to separate qualities (weight, length, tenacity) rather than the full concrete individuality; this analytic separation facilitates abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pupils to abstract by focusing on the one property relevant to a task, demonstrating how other properties can be ignored in context. Use this as an aid to generalizing and to show the utility of analytic thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize forms of knowledge that connect with pupils' wants and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that directly relates to subsistence, safety, comfort, or the higher senses and emotions is more naturally interesting and easier to learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link instruction to pupils' practical interests, feelings, or sensory attractions (food, shelter, social objects, nature, persons). Use such connections as a basis before moving to less intrinsically interesting but valuable general knowledge.
